---
title: "HMC Benchmark"
---

Source code for benchmark: [https://github.com/r-xla/benchmarks/tree/main/benchmarks/hmc](https://github.com/r-xla/benchmarks/tree/main/benchmarks/hmc).

## Experiment Setup

The benchmark compares three implementations of a fixed-trajectory **Hamiltonian Monte Carlo** sampler: **Stan** (static HMC), **R torch**, and **anvil** (with both a compiled-loop variant and an R-loop variant).
The target is the 2-D "banana" distribution

$$
U(\theta) = \frac{\theta_1^2}{200} + \frac{(\theta_2 - b\,\theta_1^2 + 100 b)^2}{2}, \qquad b = 0.01,
$$

whose marginal standard deviations are known analytically ($\mathrm{sd}(\theta_1) = 10$, $\mathrm{sd}(\theta_2) = \sqrt{1 + 2\cdot10^4 b^2} \approx 1.73$), so sampling accuracy can be measured directly.

The key axis of variation is the **number of parallel chains** $K$.
The anvil and torch samplers are written in batched form: every array carries a leading chain axis of size $K$, so all chains advance together as a single device computation.
Stan instead runs $K$ independent Markov chains, with no cross-chain vectorisation.

**Parameters:**

- **Leapfrog steps (L):** 80
- **Step size ($\epsilon$):** 0.2 (integration time $L\epsilon = 16$)
- **Samples per chain:** 1000 (after 500 warmup)
- **Mass matrix:** identity (`metric = "unit_e"` in Stan, unit momenta elsewhere)

All three samplers use the same step size, integration time, and identity mass matrix.
Stan's adaptation is disabled (`algorithm = "HMC"`, `adapt_engaged = FALSE`) so every sampler performs exactly $L$ leapfrog steps per iteration.
Timing excludes the warmup phase. For anvil, JIT compilation time is recorded separately; for Stan the (one-time) C++ model compilation is the recorded compile time.
All reported values are medians across replications.

## CPU Results

Wall time for drawing 1000 samples per chain as the number of parallel chains grows.
Because the anvil and torch kernels are batched, adding chains is nearly free until the device saturates, whereas Stan's runtime grows roughly linearly with the chain count.

![](benchmarks/hmc/hmc_benchmark.png){width=100%}

The amortized cost per pooled sample (total samples $= K \times 1000$) makes the batching advantage explicit: for the device-vectorised samplers the per-sample cost falls as more chains are run in parallel.

![](benchmarks/hmc/hmc_per_sample.png){width=100%}

All samplers target the same distribution, so their accuracy (mean relative error of the estimated marginal standard deviations against the analytic truth) is comparable and improves with more chains.

![](benchmarks/hmc/hmc_accuracy.png){width=100%}

## GPU Results

The GPU benchmark uses the same setup on CUDA over a larger range of parallel chains.
Stan has no GPU sampler and is omitted; only the device-vectorised anvil and torch implementations are compared.

![](benchmarks/hmc/hmc_benchmark_gpu.png){width=100%}

![](benchmarks/hmc/hmc_per_sample_gpu.png){width=100%}
